description: Hi! I am Asadullah Khan, a r BS Nursing graduate with a strong interest in healthcare data science and AI in healthcare. I’m leading our team for the “Create Health Monitoring Software for Astronauts on Space Missions” challenge.
summary: Astronaut Health Monitor is an interactive dashboard that turns astronaut vital signs into early, explainable warnings for long-duration missions. Most health tools show raw numbers and leave interpretation to a doctor, but crews on the Moon and Mars may be minutes to hours away from ground support. Our dashboard tracks six vital signs (heart rate, blood pressure, sleep, SpO2, body temperature, stress) over a 180-day mission, flags readings outside normal ranges, and combines them into a Normal, Warning or Critical status. Every alert is linked to a NASA Human Research Program risk, such as Hypoxia or Cardiovascular adaptations, with a suggested action for the crew medic. NASA's five spaceflight hazards are mapped to the vital signs they affect. Crew members, flight surgeons and mission planners get a plain-language view with no coding needed, and anyone can upload their own CSV, which is processed privately in the browser. The demo uses simulated data because astronaut health data is not public. It is decision support only, not medical advice.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

Astronaut Health Monitor is a web dashboard that watches crew health over a long mission and explains problems in plain language. Instead of only plotting numbers, it tells the crew what an out-of-range reading may relate to and what to do next. The gap it addresses: on missions far from Earth, crews cannot rely on real-time help from ground doctors, yet most monitoring tools present raw data that needs expert interpretation.

HOW IT WORKS

- Tracks six vital signs per astronaut over a 180-day mission: heart rate, systolic blood pressure, sleep, SpO2, body temperature and stress score.

- Compares each reading to a normal range and marks out-of-range days on a trend chart.

- Combines the signals into a daily status: Normal (0 out of range), Warning (1-2), Critical (3 or more).

- Shows active alerts, each linked to the matching NASA Human Research Program risk with a suggested crew-medic action.

- Maps NASA's five hazards of spaceflight (radiation, isolation and confinement, distance from Earth, gravity fields, hostile/closed environments) to the vital signs they affect.

- Lets users upload their own CSV of readings (one row per astronaut per day). The file is processed in the browser and never saved or sent anywhere.

KEY BENEFITS AND IMPACT

- Crew members: early, understandable warnings without needing a medical degree.

- Flight surgeons and ground teams: a quick view of who needs attention and why.

- Mission planners: a way to see which health risks matter most as missions move toward the Moon and Mars.

- Anyone with real readings can test the tool with their own data, with no coding.

DATA

NASA does not publish individual astronaut health data, so the demo uses simulated data for a four-person crew. The simulation includes planned events (a fever episode, a stress and poor-sleep trend, and a brief oxygen drop) to show the dashboard catching realistic problems. Risk links and hazard mapping come from NASA's Human Research Program pages.

TOOLS AND TECHNOLOGIES

- Lovable: web app and dashboard

- Python (pandas) and Streamlit: early prototype and data simulation

- Claude (Anthropic): planning, code, and app prompt

- Seeded random generation for repeatable simulated data

CREATIVE ELEMENTS

- Designed from a nursing perspective: metrics and alerts reflect how clinicians watch for early warning signs.

- Every alert is explainable: it names the NASA risk and a next step instead of just showing a number.

- Privacy-friendly: uploaded health data stays in the user's browser.

LIMITATIONS AND NEXT STEPS

Normal ranges are demonstration placeholders, the same for every astronaut, and would need clinical validation and personal baselines before real use. The tool does not diagnose and is not medical advice. Next steps: connect real wearable or medical-record data, add personal baselines, and add radiation dose monitoring once reliable public data is available.

USE OF ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE (AI)

We used AI tools to speed up development.

- Claude (Anthropic): helped plan the project, write and review code, create the data-simulation logic, and draft text. All content was reviewed and edited by the team.

- Lovable: generated the web app from our written prompt.

The data is simulated by code, not real. No NASA logos, flags or mission identifiers were used. The project idea, health metrics, alert logic and direction came from the team.
